The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04230
Another hadith, transmitted by al-Tirmidhī from Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī, reports the Prophet as saying:
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04231
“Gabriel came to me and gave me the good news that anyone from your community who dies without associating anything with God will enter Paradise.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04232
I said”—the speaker here is Abū Dharr—“Even if he commits adultery and steals?”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04233
He said: “Even if he commits adultery and steals.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04234
I said: “Even if he commits adultery and steals?”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04235
He said: “Even if he commits adultery and steals.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04236
Then, on the fourth time, he said: “Whether Abū Dharr likes it or not.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04237
This hadith carries the same two implications, but even more clearly.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04238
Abū Dharr is more persistent in his questioning.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04239
And the Prophet, according to the report, ends the discussion even more firmly.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04240
This attitude is reinforced and explained by another hadith, reported by the companion Umāma:
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04241
“The Messenger of God said: ‘No people went astray after having been rightly guided except when they were given to disputation.’”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04242
So where did this dislike of intellectual debate come from, and why?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04243
There were two factors: a direct factor connected with faith, and an indirect social factor.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04243
First — The Factor of Faith
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04244
Here we are dealing with the relationship between knowledge and faith.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04245
That relationship follows from the Islamic view of knowledge—the view that knowledge of doctrine and law comes from God.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04246
A decisive expression of this idea appears in the Prophet’s sermon at Ghadīr Khumm on his return from the Farewell Pilgrimage:
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04247
“Today I have perfected your religion for you, completed My blessing upon you, and chosen Islam for you as your religion.” (Qurʾān 5:3)
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04248
The verse was presented by the Prophet as words from God to the Muslims.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04249
It told them that the religion communicated by the Prophet had now been completed, and with it God’s blessing upon them: Islam as both doctrine and law.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04250

In this setting, according to the books of Qurʾānic interpretation, “perfection” and “completion” mean that everything Islam had brought in matters of belief and law was final. It was to be taken as it was, without alteration or change.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04251
This means that people received knowledge of doctrine and law as something complete, through an absolute act of faith.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04252
If people were allowed to use their own understanding to gain knowledge in this area, their role was limited mainly to understanding the texts that contained the details of doctrine and law.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04253

Even this freedom was restricted by what was believed to have been transmitted from the divine source through the Prophet, with chains of transmission ultimately judged by specialists in hadith and its transmitters.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04254
One example of this can be seen in the way Qurʾānic commentators explained the word ḥikma, or “wisdom.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04255
The word appears frequently in the Qurʾān.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04256

We know that before Islam it had carried a meaning connected with a simple kind of rational reflection. It referred to knowledge gained directly from things and to general judgments drawn from personal experience.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04257

In other words, pre-Islamic Arabs could understand “wisdom” as gaining knowledge from what could be observed through the senses and using that knowledge as a basis for thought, even if only at a very simple level.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04258
But what does the word “wisdom” mean in the Qurʾān?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04259

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, who died in 463 AH / 1070 CE, reports in his Jāmiʿ Bayān al-ʿIlm wa-Faḍlihi that Mālik explained “wisdom” in many Qurʾānic verses as understanding God’s religion and acting according to it.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04260
In his commentary on the verse,
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04261
“Remember what is recited in your homes of God’s verses and of wisdom” (Qurʾān 33:34),
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04262
al-Ṭabarī says that “wisdom” means what was revealed to the Messenger of God concerning the rules of religion but was not included in the Qurʾān itself—in other words, the Sunna.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04263
And in explaining the verse,
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04264
“He gives wisdom to whomever He wills, and whoever is given wisdom has been given great good” (Qurʾān 2:269),
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04265
Ibn ʿAbbās said that “wisdom” meant knowing the rules concerning what is permitted and what is forbidden.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04266
According to these statements and interpretations, then, “wisdom” is limited to knowledge received from an outside source—knowledge of religion as doctrine and law.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04267

We do not find here the older sense of “wisdom” as knowledge gained through the activity of reason as it deals with things, or as it draws ideas and concepts from that experience through its own powers and faculties.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04268
All of this leads us to the conclusion that the relationship between knowledge and faith is central to understanding the limits originally placed on knowledge in Islam.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04268
Second — The Social Factor
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04269
Here we need to return once again to the question of monotheism and its relation to knowledge.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04270

If we examine the Islamic idea of monotheism more deeply, from its different historical sides and dimensions, we are led to another question: the basic relationship between Islamic belief and Islamic law, and therefore the social basis of that relationship.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04271
Separating belief from law is not only a methodological mistake. It also goes against the logic of the Islamic mission itself.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04272
That logic joined faith to a social order. Faith functioned as the ideology of that order. The two were connected rather than separate.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04273
We therefore have to understand monotheism through this connection.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04274
It was the point at which the historical role of Islam came together.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04275
Religious unity could not be separated from social unity.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04276
The two depended on one another.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04277

Their agreement was necessary for both to exist, and their existence together was necessary for the creation of a unified social framework replacing—or historically required to replace—the divided tribal structure of the time.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04278
Seen in this way, we can understand how monotheism affected the question of knowledge.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04279
Placing knowledge within the relationship between faith and understanding, and restricting its ultimate source to God, was the intellectual side of the principle of unity.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04280
In other words, it was the ideological side of monotheism.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04281
Ultimately, it was the ideological expression of a unified social institution.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04282
Seen from this perspective, the early reluctance to engage in intellectual debate becomes easier to understand.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04283
During the Prophet’s lifetime and through most of the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, the conditions existed for this reluctance to remain firm while still retaining some practical flexibility.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04284
But after the killing of the third caliph, ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, those conditions began to weaken.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04285
Social and political contradictions were becoming more developed and were turning, at an increasing rate, into open conflicts.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04286
From this historical turning point onward, reluctance toward intellectual debate could no longer stand on the same firm ground as before.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04287
Intellectual debate began actively making its way into social and political conflict despite the powerful material and ideological forces trying to restrain it.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04288
2 — Testimony from Muslim Scholars
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04289
The picture of knowledge in Islam that we have just described is also supported by statements made by Muslim religious scholars.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04290
We may remember, for example, the passage quoted earlier from the judge Ṣāʿid al-Andalusī in his Ṭabaqāt al-Umam:
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04291
“As for the science of philosophy, God Almighty did not grant them anything of it...”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04292
This statement clearly presents knowledge as something given to human beings by God, rather than something people gain through the effort of their own minds.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04293
Al-Ghazālī gives us another example.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04294
While explaining his position on the discipline of kalām, or speculative theology, he says:
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04295

“Its purpose—that is, the purpose of kalām—is only to preserve the creed of the Sunna and protect it from the confusion caused by the people of innovation. God Almighty gave His servants, through the words of His Messenger, a creed that is the truth and that serves the good of their religion and worldly life, as the Qurʾān and the reports of the Prophet make known. Then Satan planted in the minds of the innovators ideas opposed to the Sunna. They became absorbed in them and nearly disturbed the true belief of its followers. So God brought forth a group of theologians and stirred in them the motives to defend the Sunna...”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04296
Al-Ghazālī does not merely say that Islamic beliefs were given by God “through His Messenger.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04297
He goes further.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04298
He says that Satan put the ideas of the innovators into their minds, and that God brought the theologians into being and inspired them to defend the Sunna.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04299
On this view, even rational knowledge—and especially philosophical knowledge—reaches theologians and philosophers from outside their own minds and powers of understanding.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04300
Its source is either God or Satan.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04301
Ibn Khaldūn also understood the question of knowledge in Islam in this way when he said that “reason is excluded from religious law and its investigations.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04302
Ibn Taymiyya likewise says that the Muslims of early Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04303

“believed that debate and argument about matters of belief led people away from religion. For this reason, when the Prophet died, the Muslims held one creed, apart from those who secretly practiced hypocrisy. Investigation and argument over matters of belief did not appear until the time of the Companions, when innovations and doubts arose and Muslims were forced to answer them. From this came the different sects, and the discipline of kalām arose as an argument against innovators who had departed from the path of the early Muslims and opposed religion. Kalām therefore arose as a necessity and was to be used only to the extent that necessity required.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04304

This has led some modern researchers to observe that because the Qurʾān discouraged believers from investigation and argument in matters of religion, it was natural for religious scholars later to become uncomfortable with free rational inquiry whenever it extended into religious beliefs, examined them intellectually, or reached conclusions different from those the scholars were used to.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04305
This may also help explain their hostility toward philosophy and their attacks on philosophers.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04306
Another modern Muslim researcher makes a similar point.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04307

He says that the early Muslims were not occupied with “the heavens”—meaning they did not debate matters of belief—because the Qurʾān had spared them that burden by setting out the foundations of belief for them.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04308
It did not ask them to enter into questions about the causes of existence, “that tree whose branches spread in every direction.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04309
The people of the Qurʾān therefore did not go beyond its boundaries. They stopped with it and remained within it.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04310
What matters to us here is that this supports the picture we described earlier.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04311

Among the earliest Muslims, the belief that knowledge in these matters came only from God led either to a prohibition on rational debate over matters of faith or to a willingness to avoid such debate.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04312
What had already been given completely through divine revelation and prophecy was considered sufficient.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04313
Something else is worth noticing.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04314
Historians and scholars of kalām have pointed out that even during the period when this discipline flourished, theologians disagreed about the exact role of reason.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04315
They agreed that kalām used rational investigation in dealing with religious beliefs.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04316
But they disagreed over another question.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04317
Did kalām actually prove those beliefs through rational arguments as well as defend them?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04318
Or was its role limited to answering objections against beliefs already established by the Qurʾān and Sunna?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04319
These researchers explain that the disagreement came down to a deeper question:
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04320
Were religious beliefs established by revealed law—that is, by revelation—with reason merely understanding them from revelation and then finding rational arguments in their support?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04321
Or were they established by reason itself, in the sense that the religious texts had already stated those beliefs together with their rational proofs?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04322

We mention this observation because it strongly shows that even when rational inquiry flourished in the hands of the theologians, the theologians themselves remained tied to the earlier view of knowledge.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04323
As the observation above shows, they still accepted one of two positions.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04324
Either religious beliefs were established by revealed law and reason understood them through that revelation.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04325
Or they were “established by reason,” but only in the sense that the religious texts had already laid down the rational arguments for them.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04326
Even the second position therefore assumes that the rational proofs themselves were already given in advance by religious texts.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
passage-en-04327

If we look for the social and ideological basis of this position in its two forms, we find it in the need to preserve and strengthen the ideology of the new social group whose position in the developing social and class structure was supported by the idea that knowledge rested on faith.
